hook: Read two classic comic poems closely and say exactly why they are funny: the device, the rhyme and what it all adds up to.
intro: A poetry reading with two complete short poems and a commentary. Poem 1: Joachim Ringelnatz (1883–1934), „Die Ameisen“ – six lines, one stanza. Poem 2: Christian Morgenstern (1871–1914), „Das ästhetische Wiesel“ – eleven short lines in four stanzas, in its original spelling (Wißt ihr). Both texts are in the public domain because their authors died more than 70 years ago, so they can be quoted in full. The third part is NOT a poem but a commentary written for this course, „Die Komik der Unverhältnismäßigkeit“, which compares the two. Reading poetry closely means three things: seeing the device (disproportion, irony, understatement, self-reference), naming the form (rhyme scheme, stanza, line break) and stating a reading. The vocabulary of poetry analysis: das Reimschema (Paarreim aabb, Kreuzreim abab, umarmender Reim abba, Schweifreim aabccb), die Strophe, der Vers, die Pointe, die Ironie, die Untertreibung, das Missverhältnis, die Fallhöhe. The questions ask about both poems and about what the commentary says – check every form claim against the poem itself.
tips[0].title: Find the disproportion (Fallhöhe)
tips[0].text: Comic poems often set a huge claim against a tiny result. In Ringelnatz the claim is geographical (Australien vs Altona, next door to Hamburg); in Morgenstern it is rhetorical (a solemn riddle, a banal solution).
tips[0].check.why: The Fallhöhe lies between the mighty roar and the tiny result: one startled mouse.
tips[1].title: Irony and understatement in single words
tips[1].text: „weise“ – the ants are not wise; they failed and call it a decision (irony). „den letzten Teil der Reise“ – the last part is almost all of it (understatement). An interpretation names the word and says what it does.
tips[1].trap: Reading „weise“ literally turns the poem into a fable about prudence. The tiny distance and the sore legs settle it: irony.
tips[1].check.why: Three hours of rain leave everything soaked; calling it a little damp says far less than is meant.
tips[2].title: Name the form – and check it line by line
tips[2].text: Mark the last word of every line and give each new sound a letter. Ringelnatz: Ameisen/reisen, Chaussee/weh, weise/Reise = aabbcc (Paarreim), one stanza. Morgenstern: Wiesel/Kiesel/Bachgeriesel = aaa; later the rhymes jump across stanza breaks (ihr – mir – raffinier- – Tier, weshalb – Mondkalb, Stillen – willen), and a word is split at the line end to make a rhyme.
tips[2].check.why: Haus/Maus and Baum/Traum alternate: abab is a Kreuzreim.
tips[3].title: Device – form – reading: the three-sentence interpretation
tips[3].text: 1 Das Gedicht lebt von … 2 Die Form (…) unterstreicht … 3 So lässt sich das Gedicht als … deuten. The commentary in this quiz follows the same pattern – use it as a model.
tips[3].check.why: The third step says what the poem means (als … deuten); the others name the form and the device.

remember[0]: Ringelnatz: Missverhältnis im Stoff – Ironie (weise), Untertreibung (der letzte Teil), Paarreim aabbcc, eine Strophe.
remember[1]: Morgenstern: Missverhältnis in der Sprache – dreifacher Reim (aaa), Scheinrätsel, getrenntes Wort „raffinier-“ für den Reim: der Reim erzeugt den Inhalt.
remember[2]: Common ground: die Fallhöhe zwischen großem Anspruch und kleinem Ergebnis.
remember[3]: Quote only public-domain poets (authors dead for more than 70 years) and quote them exactly.
exam: Short poems with a commentary can appear in C2 exam reading; the same close attention serves any German poem you meet.
tips[0].check.q: „Der Löwe brüllte, dass die Berge bebten – und eine Maus erschrak.“ Where is the comic disproportion?
tips[0].check.options[0]: A huge effect is announced, a tiny one follows.
tips[0].check.options[1]: The lion is afraid of the mouse.
tips[0].check.answer: A huge effect is announced, a tiny one follows.
